claim: Molecular mimicry is an evolutionary strategy adopted by viruses to exploit the host cellular machinery.
source: Molecular mimicry is an evolutionary strategy adopted by viruses to exploit the host cellular machinery.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about viral evolutionary strategies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has evolved a unique S1/S2 cleavage site that is absent in any previous coronavirus sequenced.
source: We report that SARS-CoV-2 has evolved a unique S1/S2 cleavage site, absent in any previous coronavirus sequenced, resulting in the striking mimicry of an identical FURIN-cleavable peptide on the human epithelial sodium channel α-subunit (ENaC-α).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data comparing SARS-CoV-2 with other coronaviruses and analysis of coronavirus databases.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 S1/S2 cleavage site mimics an identical FURIN-cleavable peptide on human ENaC-α.
source: We report that SARS-CoV-2 has evolved a unique S1/S2 cleavage site, absent in any previous coronavirus sequenced, resulting in the striking mimicry of an identical FURIN-cleavable peptide on the human epithelial sodium channel α-subunit (ENaC-α).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison data showing the identical peptide sequence between SARS-CoV-2 and ENaC-α.

claim: Genetic alteration of ENaC-α causes aldosterone dysregulation in patients.
source: Genetic alteration of ENaC-α causes aldosterone dysregulation in patients, highlighting that the FURIN site is critical for activation of ENaC.
evidence: This claim references established clinical knowledge about ENaC-α mutations and their effects.

claim: The FURIN site is critical for activation of ENaC.
source: Genetic alteration of ENaC-α causes aldosterone dysregulation in patients, highlighting that the FURIN site is critical for activation of ENaC.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic alteration data and supported by literature on ENaC activation.

claim: There is significant overlap between expression of ENaC-α and ACE2 in cell types linked to cardiovascular-renal-pulmonary pathophysiology of COVID-19.
source: Single cell RNA-seq from 66 studies shows significant overlap between expression of ENaC-α and the viral receptor ACE2 in cell types linked to the cardiovascular-renal-pulmonary pathophysiology of COVID-19.
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data analysis from 66 studies.

claim: Proteolytic degeneracy is wired into the SARS-CoV-2 lifecycle.
source: Triangulating this cellular characterization with cleavage signatures of 178 proteases highlights proteolytic degeneracy wired into the SARS-CoV-2 lifecycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of 178 protease cleavage signatures and their relationship to SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Evolution of SARS-CoV-2 into a global pandemic may be driven in part by its targeted mimicry of ENaC-α.
source: Evolution of SARS-CoV-2 into a global pandemic may be driven in part by its targeted mimicry of ENaC-α, a protein critical for the homeostasis of airway surface liquid, whose misregulation is associated with respiratory conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the molecular mimicry findings and the role of ENaC-α in respiratory function.

claim: ENaC-α is critical for the homeostasis of airway surface liquid.
source: Evolution of SARS-CoV-2 into a global pandemic may be driven in part by its targeted mimicry of ENaC-α, a protein critical for the homeostasis of airway surface liquid, whose misregulation is associated with respiratory conditions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ENaC-α function.

claim: Misregulation of ENaC-α is associated with respiratory conditions.
source: Evolution of SARS-CoV-2 into a global pandemic may be driven in part by its targeted mimicry of ENaC-α, a protein critical for the homeostasis of airway surface liquid, whose misregulation is associated with respiratory conditions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ENaC-α and respiratory disease.

claim: The S-protein is key to the SARS-CoV-2 infection lifecycle through proteolysis.
source: The surface of SARS-CoV-2 virions is coated with the spike (S) glycoprotein, whose proteolysis is key to the infection lifecycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 infection mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: The S1 subunit of the S-protein engages ACE2 receptor.
source: After the initial interaction of the S-protein with the ACE2 receptor (Walls et al., 2020), host cell entry is mediated by two key proteolytic steps. The S1 subunit of the S-protein engages ACE2, and viral entry into the host cell is facilitated by proteases that catalyze S1/S2 cleavage (Belouzard et al., 2012; Belouzard et al., 2009) at Arginine-667/Serine-668 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on SARS-CoV-2 entry mechanisms.

claim: Viral entry into the host cell is facilitated by proteases that catalyze S1/S2 cleavage at Arginine-667/Serine-668.
source: The S1 subunit of the S-protein engages ACE2, and viral entry into the host cell is facilitated by proteases that catalyze S1/S2 cleavage (Belouzard et al., 2012; Belouzard et al., 2009) at Arginine-667/Serine-668 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and structural data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: S2' site cleavage is required for fusion of viral-host cell membranes.
source: This is followed by S2' site cleavage that is required for fusion of viral-host cell membranes (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on SARS-CoV-2 membrane fusion.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has evolved a unique sequence insertion at the S1/S2 site compared to SARS-CoV, Pangolin-CoV, and Bat-CoV RaTG13.
source: Comparing human-infecting SARS-CoV-2 with SARS-CoV strains, as well as with candidates of zoonotic origin (Pangolin-CoV and Bat-CoV RaTG13), shows that SARS-CoV-2 has evolved a unique sequence insertion at the S1/S2 site (Zhang et al., 2020; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1a and cited literature.

claim: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shares 92% sequence identity with Pangolin-CoV S protein.
source: Although the S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shares high sequence identity with the S proteins of Pangolin-CoV (92%) and Bat-CoV RaTG13 (97%), the furin insertion site seems to be uniquely acquired by SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: The S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shares 97% sequence identity with Bat-CoV RaTG13 S protein.
source: Although the S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shares high sequence identity with the S proteins of Pangolin-CoV (92%) and Bat-CoV RaTG13 (97%), the furin insertion site seems to be uniquely acquired by SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: The furin insertion site is uniquely acquired by SARS-CoV-2.
source: Although the S protein of SARS-CoV-2 shares high sequence identity with the S proteins of Pangolin-CoV (92%) and Bat-CoV RaTG13 (97%), the furin insertion site seems to be uniquely acquired by SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence comparison data showing the absence of this site in related coronaviruses.

claim: The tribasic 8-mer peptide RRARSVAS at the SARS-CoV-2 S1/S2 site is conserved among 10,956 of 10,967 circulating strains deposited at GISAID as of April 28, 2020.
source: The resulting tribasic 8-mer peptide (RRARSVAS) on the SARS-CoV-2 S1/S2 site is conserved among 10,956 of 10,967 circulating strains deposited at GISAID (https://www.gisaid.org/) (Elbe and Buckland-Merrett, 2017), as of April 28, 2020 (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sequence data from the GISAID database.

claim: The RRARSVAS peptide is absent in over 13,000 non-COVID-19 coronavirus S-proteins from the VIPR database.
source: This peptide is also absent in over 13,000 non-COVID-19 coronavirus S-proteins from the VIPR database (Carrillo-Tripp et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on database analysis of coronavirus sequences.

claim: The peptide RRARSVAS is present exclusively in human ENaC-α among over 10 million peptides from 20,350 canonical human proteins in UniProtKB with p-value=4E-4.
source: Strikingly, examining over 10 million peptides (8-mers) of 20,350 canonical human proteins from UniProtKB shows that the peptide of interest (RRARSVAS) is present exclusively in human ENaC-ɑ, also known as SCNN1A (p-value=4E-4) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the human proteome database.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 mimicked peptide in ENaC-α is located in the extracellular domain.
source: The location of this SARS-CoV-2 mimicked peptide in the ENaC-ɑ structure is in the extracellular domain (Noreng et al., 2018; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by structural data from cited literature and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may have specifically evolved to mimic a human protease substrate.
source: This suggests that the SARS-CoV-2 may have specifically evolved to mimic a human protease substrate.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the molecular mimicry findings.

claim: ENaC regulates sodium ion and water homeostasis.
source: ENaC regulates sodium ion (Na+) and water homeostasis, and ENaC's expression levels are controlled by aldosterone and the associated Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)6.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ENaC function.

claim: ENaC's expression levels are controlled by aldosterone and the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).
source: ENaC regulates sodium ion (Na+) and water homeostasis, and ENaC's expression levels are controlled by aldosterone and the associated Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)6.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ENaC regulation.

claim: ENaC plays a key role in controlling fluid reabsorption at the air-liquid interface in distal lung airways.
source: In distal lung airways, ENaC is known to play a key role in controlling fluid reabsorption at the air–liquid interface (Rossier and Stutts, 2009), and similar to SARS-CoV2, ENaC-ɑ also needs to be proteolytically activated for its function (Vallet et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on ENaC function in the lungs.

claim: ENaC-α needs to be proteolytically activated for its function.
source: In distal lung airways, ENaC is known to play a key role in controlling fluid reabsorption at the air–liquid interface (Rossier and Stutts, 2009), and similar to SARS-CoV2, ENaC-ɑ also needs to be proteolytically activated for its function (Vallet et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on ENaC activation.

claim: FURIN cleaves the equivalent peptide on mouse ENaC-α between the Arginine and Serine residues in the 4th and 5th positions respectively (RSAR|SASS).
source: FURIN cleaves the equivalent peptide on mouse ENaC-ɑ between the Arginine and Serine residues in the 4th and 5th positions respectively (RSAR|SASS) (Hughey et al., 2004a; Hughey et al., 2004b), akin to the recent report establishing FURIN cleavage at the S1/S2 site of SARS-CoV-2 (Walls et al., 2020; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on FURIN cleavage of mouse ENaC-α.

claim: FURIN cleaves at the S1/S2 site of SARS-CoV-2.
source: FURIN cleaves the equivalent peptide on mouse ENaC-ɑ between the Arginine and Serine residues in the 4th and 5th positions respectively (RSAR|SASS) (Hughey et al., 2004a; Hughey et al., 2004b), akin to the recent report establishing FURIN cleavage at the S1/S2 site of SARS-CoV-2 (Walls et al., 2020; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on SARS-CoV-2 cleavage.

claim: Human ENaC activation may be compromised in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells by the virus exploiting host FURIN for its own activation.
source: It is conceivable that human ENaC activation may be compromised in SARS-CoV-2 infected cells, for instance by SARS-CoV-2 exploiting host FURIN for its own activation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the molecular mimicry findings.

claim: Low ENaC activity on the surface of airways leads to compromised fluid reabsorption.
source: The likely consequence would be low ENaC activity on the surface of the airways leading to compromised fluid reabsorption (Planès et al., 2010; Yurdakök, 2010), an important lung pathology in COVID-19 patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on ENaC function and lung pathology.

claim: Compromised fluid reabsorption is an important lung pathology in COVID-19 patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
source: The likely consequence would be low ENaC activity on the surface of the airways leading to compromised fluid reabsorption (Planès et al., 2010; Yurdakök, 2010), an important lung pathology in COVID-19 patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
evidence: This is based on clinical observations of COVID-19 pathology and cited literature.

claim: Furin-like cleavage motifs can be found in other viruses.
source: Although the furin-like cleavage motifs can be found in other viruses (Coutard et al., 2020), the exact mimicry of human ENaC-ɑ cleavage site raises the specter that SARS-CoV-2 may be hijacking the protease network of ENaC-ɑ for viral activation.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on viral cleavage motifs.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may be hijacking the protease network of ENaC-α for viral activation.
source: Although the furin-like cleavage motifs can be found in other viruses (Coutard et al., 2020), the exact mimicry of human ENaC-ɑ cleavage site raises the specter that SARS-CoV-2 may be hijacking the protease network of ENaC-ɑ for viral activation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the molecular mimicry findings.

claim: ENaC-α is expressed in nasal epithelial cells.
source: Interestingly, ENaC-ɑ is expressed in the nasal epithelial cells, type II alveolar cells of the lungs, tongue keratinocytes, and colon enterocytes (Figure 1c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6), which are all implicated in COVID-19 pathophysiology (Shweta et al., 2020; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: ENaC-α is expressed in type II alveolar cells of the lungs.
source: Interestingly, ENaC-ɑ is expressed in the nasal epithelial cells, type II alveolar cells of the lungs, tongue keratinocytes, and colon enterocytes (Figure 1c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6), which are all implicated in COVID-19 pathophysiology (Shweta et al., 2020; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: ENaC-α is expressed in tongue keratinocytes.
source: Interestingly, ENaC-ɑ is expressed in the nasal epithelial cells, type II alveolar cells of the lungs, tongue keratinocytes, and colon enterocytes (Figure 1c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6), which are all implicated in COVID-19 pathophysiology (Shweta et al., 2020; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: ENaC-α is expressed in colon enterocytes.
source: Interestingly, ENaC-ɑ is expressed in the nasal epithelial cells, type II alveolar cells of the lungs, tongue keratinocytes, and colon enterocytes (Figure 1c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6), which are all implicated in COVID-19 pathophysiology (Shweta et al., 2020; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by single cell RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claim: Nasal epithelial cells, type II alveolar cells of the lungs, tongue keratinocytes, and colon enterocytes are all implicated in COVID-19 pathophysiology.
source: Interestingly, ENaC-ɑ is expressed in the nasal epithelial cells, type II alveolar cells of the lungs, tongue keratinocytes, and colon enterocytes (Figure 1c and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–6), which are all implicated in COVID-19 pathophysiology (Shweta et al., 2020; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on COVID-19 pathophysiology.

claim: ACE2 and ENaC-α are expressed in the apical membranes of polarized epithelial cells.
source: Further, ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ are known to be expressed generally in the apical membranes of polarized epithelial cells (Butterworth, 2010; Musante et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on cellular localization of ACE2 and ENaC-α.

claim: The overlap of cell-types expressing ACE2 and ENaC-α suggests that SARS-CoV-2 may be leveraging the protease network responsible for ENaC cleavage.
source: The overlap of the cell-types expressing ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ, and similar spatial distributions at the apical surfaces, suggest that SARS-CoV-2 may be leveraging the protease network responsible for ENaC cleavage.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the co-expression data.

claim: FURIN (PCSK3) has overall proteolytic similarity to PCSK5 (0.99), PCSK7 (0.99), PCSK6 (0.99), PCSK4 (0.98), and PCSK2 (0.94).
source: This shows that FURIN (PCSK3) has overall proteolytic similarity to select PCSK family members, specifically PCSK5 (0.99), PCSK7 (0.99), PCSK6 (0.99), PCSK4 (0.98), and PCSK2 (0.94) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of protease cleavage specificity using a cosine similarity metric.

claim: The protease PLG cleaves the γ-subunit of ENaC (ENaC-γ).
source: It is also known that the protease PLG cleaves the ɣ-subunit of ENaC (ENaC-ɣ)(Passero et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on ENaC cleavage.

claim: FURIN is expressed with ACE2 and ENaC-α in the colon (immature enterocytes, transit amplifying cells) and pancreas (ductal cells, acinar cells) of human tissues.
source: This analysis shows that FURIN is expressed with ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ in the colon (immature enterocytes, transit amplifying cells) and pancreas (ductal cells, acinar cells) of human tissues, as well as tongue (keratinocytes) of mouse tissues.
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq co-expression analysis.

claim: FURIN is expressed with ACE2 and ENaC-α in tongue keratinocytes of mouse tissues.
source: This analysis shows that FURIN is expressed with ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ in the colon (immature enterocytes, transit amplifying cells) and pancreas (ductal cells, acinar cells) of human tissues, as well as tongue (keratinocytes) of mouse tissues.
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq co-expression analysis.

claim: PCSK5 and PCSK7 are broadly expressed across multiple cell types with ACE2 and ENaC-α.
source: PCSK5 and PCSK7 are broadly expressed across multiple cell types with ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ, making it a plausible broad-spectrum protease that may cleave the S1/S2 site.
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq co-expression analysis.

claim: PCSK5 and PCSK7 are plausible broad-spectrum proteases that may cleave the S1/S2 site.
source: PCSK5 and PCSK7 are broadly expressed across multiple cell types with ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ, making it a plausible broad-spectrum protease that may cleave the S1/S2 site.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the co-expression data and proteolytic similarity.

claim: PCSK6 is expressed concomitant with ACE2 and ENaC-α in cells from the intestines, pancreas, and lungs in humans.
source: In humans, concomitant with ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ, PCSK6 appears to be expressed in cells from the intestines, pancreas, and lungs, whereas PCSK2 is noted to be co-expressed in the pancreas (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq co-expression analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: PCSK2 is co-expressed with ACE2 and ENaC-α in the pancreas in humans.
source: In humans, concomitant with ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ, PCSK6 appears to be expressed in cells from the intestines, pancreas, and lungs, whereas PCSK2 is noted to be co-expressed in the pancreas (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq co-expression analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Extracellular proteases need not necessarily be expressed in the same cells as ACE2 and ENaC-α.
source: It is worth noting that the extracellular proteases need not necessarily be expressed in the same cells as ACE2 and ENaC-ɑ.
evidence: This is a statement based on biological knowledge about extracellular protease function.

claim: Redundancy may be wired into the mechanisms of host proteolytic activation of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Our findings emphasize that redundancy may be wired into the mechanisms of host proteolytic activation of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis showing multiple proteases with similar cleavage specificity.

claim: The mimicry of a cleavable host peptide central to pulmonary, renal, and cardiovascular function provides a new perspective to the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 in causing a global coronavirus pandemic.
source: The mimicry of a cleavable host peptide central to pulmonary, renal, and cardiovascular function provides a new perspective to the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 in causing a global coronavirus pandemic.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the molecular mimicry findings in the context of pandemic evolution.

claim: The analysis examined approximately 1.3 million cells from 66 single cell RNA-seq studies.
source: Systematic single cell expression profiling of the ACE2 receptor and ENaC-ɑ was performed across human and mouse samples comprising ~1.3 million cells (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2020; Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the analysis.

claim: 10,257,893 8-mers were enumerated from 20,350 reviewed uniprot reference sequences from human proteome.
source: We enumerated 10,257,893 (10.26M) 8-mers from 20,350 reviewed uniprot reference sequences from human proteome (Proteome ID: UP000005640, as accessed on May 4th 2020).
evidence: This describes the computational analysis performed on the human proteome.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 8-mer 'RRARSVAS' was found in ENaC-α protein (Uniprot ID: P37088) with p-value approximately 4E-4.
source: The previously identified SARS-CoV-2 8-mer 'RRARSVAS' was in fact found in ENaC-ɑ protein (Uniprot ID: P37088; p-value ≈ 10.26M/208 = 4E-4; chance of finding that particular 8-mer anywhere in the reference sequences).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the human proteome database.

claim: ACE2 expression could be detected in 66 studies spanning approximately 50 tissues, over 450 cell-types and approximately 1.05 million cells.
source: The ACE2 expression could be detected in 66 studies (59 studies of human samples and 7 studies of mouse samples) spanning across ~50 tissues, over 450 cell-types and ~1.05 million cells.
evidence: This describes the scope of the single cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: A genetic alteration on human ENaC-α results in a frameshift mutation causing S205X truncation leading to Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA 1).
source: One of the known genetic alterations on human ENaC-ɑ is highlighted as well (Welzel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b with citation to Welzel et al., 2013, indicating a frameshift mutation resulting in S205X truncation causing Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA 1).

claim: Only 2.77% of proximal tubule cells had detectable expression of SCNN1A (ENaC-α).
source: Although only 2.77% of the proximal tubule cells had detectable expression of SCNN1A, a higher percentage (8.46%) of these cells were also observed to express ACE2 (Primary data processed from Pubmed ID: 31604275 and hosted on https://academia.nferx.com/).
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: 8.46% of proximal tubule cells express ACE2.
source: Although only 2.77% of the proximal tubule cells had detectable expression of SCNN1A, a higher percentage (8.46%) of these cells were also observed to express ACE2 (Primary data processed from Pubmed ID: 31604275 and hosted on https://academia.nferx.com/).
evidence: This is based on single cell RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.
